name: Sunless tan injections ('tan jabs')
lead: "Tan jabs" are unlicensed injectable products, usually called melanotan, sold online and in some gyms and salons to darken skin without sun exposure. They are synthetic analogues of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (alpha-MSH), which drives melanin production.[1][2]

They have never been approved as tanning drugs. Health agencies began warning against them in 2007, and the US FDA issued a warning letter in 2009.[2] A 2009 BMJ report linked an unlicensed "sun tan jab" to changes in moles.[3] Related approved drugs exist for other uses: afamelanotide for a rare light-sensitivity disorder, and bremelanotide for hypoactive sexual desire disorder in premenopausal women.[1]

paras: Alpha-MSH's role in pigmentation was known from the 1960s, and University of Arizona researchers developed analogues in the 1980s, including melanotan I (afamelanotide).[1] Melanotan II was later licensed to Palatin for sexual dysfunction, with development dropped around 2000 in favour of bremelanotide.[2]

Reported effects include facial flushing, nausea, vomiting, yawning and appetite loss, and erections in men.[2] The 2009 BMJ report described changes to moles linked to an unlicensed tan jab.[3] Moles and freckles may darken.[2] Evidence on melanoma is unclear: a 2013 review found no conclusive proof of a causal link, and a 2021 review suggested higher melanoma rates among users could probably be explained by greater UV exposure.[2] Warnings were issued by agencies including the Danish Medicines Agency, UK MHRA, US FDA, Irish Medicines Board and Norwegian Medicines Agency.[2]
No studies found for unlicensed tanning use. The 2009 BMJ item is a case report of mole changes.[3]

timeline.event: University of Arizona researchers develop alpha-MSH analogues.[1]
Health agencies begin warning against unlicensed products.[2]
BMJ report on mole changes; FDA warning letter.[2][3]
FDA approves bremelanotide for a sexual desire disorder.[1]

card.summary: Unlicensed melanotan injections for tanning; flagged by health agencies since 2007 and linked to mole changes.
card.note: Not legal to sell for human use; agencies have issued warnings.

quick.overview:
Tan jabs are unlicensed melanotan injections sold to darken skin without sun exposure.

Health agencies in several countries have warned against them since 2007.
quick.mechanism: Melanotan peptides mimic alpha-MSH and stimulate melanin production.[1][2]
quick.risks: Reported effects include flushing, nausea and mole darkening or changes;[2][3] melanoma evidence is unclear. They are unlicensed for tanning.
